messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
Marisol, a 38-year-old Latin American community organizer, came to treatment after years of carrying childhood abuse in a way that had become more and more costly in her present life. She had grown up with a caregiver who could corner her in a kitchen, a hallway, or a bedroom and make it clear that there was no way out; as an adult, the feeling of having no options still hit her with startling force. At work she would scan a meeting room before sitting, choosing the chair with the clearest view of the door or the seat that let her keep her back to a wall. On the bus home she found herself checking behind her at crosswalks and in shop windows, and at night she struggled to fall asleep because she needed to stay alert, as if lowering her guard might invite danger back in. When she felt trapped by a crowded conference table, a stalled conversation with a tenant, or even a packed subway car, she threw herself into tasks, answered emails late into the evening, and tried to erase the whole thing from her mind. The more she pushed herself to keep moving, the less room there seemed to be for anything else, yet the memories still intruded.

Those moments of entrapment did not remain abstract. They carried her straight back to brief, image-like flashes of the abuse: a hand raised in a narrow doorway, the pattern on a carpet, the edge of a table, the way one side of the room disappeared from view. Marisol described her memory of the event as mostly pictures or images, with some moments extremely clear and others completely blank, and said that sometimes she could recall what happened only with a strange numbness, as if it had happened to someone else. Those fragments arrived suddenly while she was setting up folding chairs for a neighborhood meeting or waiting in line at the pharmacy, and the suddenness made her feel even more cornered. A smell, a tone of voice, or the simple discomfort of being too close to someone in a small room could pull her back into it. She would immediately look for the safest seat, sit with her back against a wall, or leave herself extra work to do so she would not have to stay with the image. Even after she tried to push the memory away, the pictures seemed to sharpen and return, often in the very places where she had hoped to forget them.

Over time, Marisol had come to believe that her reactions meant something bad about her. She told herself, with a flatness that sounded rehearsed, that she was weak, and that somebody else would have stopped the abuse from happening. That belief made the old scenes feel less like injuries and more like evidence against her. It also made her more watchful: if she was weak, then she had to compensate by anticipating every risk, by constantly checking behind her, by selecting seats based on how protected she felt, by scanning every room for escape routes. The problem was that this vigilance kept her close to the very sensations that set her off, and the more alert she became, the more the memory seemed to gather force. A sudden image would come to mind in the middle of a staff meeting, and with it came the thought that she was dead inside, cut off from feeling in a way that confirmed how damaged she believed herself to be. That numbness did not soothe her. It frightened her, because it seemed to prove that she could be overwhelmed again without even knowing it in time.

As the months passed, the strategies she used to keep herself steady began to narrow her world. She stayed late at the community center to avoid taking the subway home with its unpredictable crowding. She volunteered for extra shifts and administrative tasks because being busy was safer than sitting still with her mind. She sat with her back to walls in restaurants, office trainings, and even family gatherings, and if she could not arrange that, she became restless and distracted. Yet these habits kept bringing the memories closer, not farther away. The more she tried to erase the event, the more vividly it returned in pictures; the more she organized her days around avoiding discomfort, the more often ordinary places started to feel like places where she had once been trapped. A crowded rally could make her suddenly feel hemmed in, and that sense of no options would revive the same urgent scanning, the same need to check behind her, the same certainty that she must never let herself relax. By the time she reached out for help, Marisol was exhausted by living as though she had to remain braced for an attack she knew could come from nowhere. What brought her in was the fear that this way of living was becoming permanent, and what she most hoped for was to stop feeling dead inside and to believe, for the first time, that she was not weak, and that the past did not have to keep deciding where she could sit, sleep, or go.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette does not clearly show triggering cues directly causing the maladaptive strategies in the same paragraph, rather than simply co-occurring.
  e.g. "She stopped taking that route to work entirely — better to add twenty minutes to her commute than to feel that way again."
  e.g. "When the anniversary came around, she kept herself moving all day, cleaning, cooking, anything, because sitting still meant the thoughts would catch up."
  e.g. "She started leaving events early, telling herself she was tired, because staying too long meant the chances of something going wrong only multiplied."
- Triggers → Memory: The vignette shows reminders bringing back images, but not a clear trigger-to-memory causal link in the same paragraph for all relevant instances.
  e.g. "The smell of his cologne in the lift sent the whole night flooding back before she had even reached her floor."
  e.g. "Hearing that song on the radio dragged her straight back into the room where it happened, as if no time had passed at all."
  e.g. "Walking past the bus stop where it occurred, she was no longer on the street — she was back there, every detail sharp and close."
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not explicitly state that triggers lead to negative appraisals.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: It does not clearly state that negative appraisals drive the traumatic memory or recollection.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Memory → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette does not clearly show the memory itself leading to the maladaptive coping behaviors in the same paragraph.
  e.g. "She had learned that if she kept the television on loud enough, the thoughts couldn't get a foothold — silence was the enemy."
  e.g. "After the memory surfaced during sex, she began finding quiet reasons to avoid intimacy altogether, telling herself she was simply tired or stressed."
  e.g. "To stop the images coming at night, she started staying up later and later, until exhaustion was the only reliable way to fall asleep."
- Memory → Triggers: It does not clearly establish that the memory itself functions as a trigger for later reactions in the required causal sense across a paragraph.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Memory: The vignette does not clearly show threat causing the memory to emerge.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: It does not clearly show perceived threat leading to negative appraisals.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Threat → Triggers: The vignette does not clearly show threat directly producing triggers/reminders.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: It does not clearly show that the maladaptive strategies themselves cause the memory to return.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: It does not clearly show that the maladaptive strategies themselves generate triggers/reminders.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
At work she would scan a meeting room before sitting, choosing the chair with the clearest view of the door or the seat that let her keep her back to a wall. On the bus home she found herself checking behind her at crosswalks and in shop windows, and at night she struggled to fall asleep because she needed to stay alert, as if lowering her guard might invite danger back in.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
When a crowded conference table, a stalled conversation with a tenant, or even a packed subway car made her feel trapped, she immediately threw herself into tasks, answered emails late into the evening, and tried to stay constantly busy; being in those places lit up the old feeling of no way out, and her first move was to create distance from it.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Those moments of entrapment did not remain abstract. They carried her straight back to brief, image-like flashes of the abuse: a hand raised in a narrow doorway, the pattern on a carpet, the edge of a table, the way one side of the room disappeared from view.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
A narrow hallway, a doorway that felt too tight, or the sight of a table edge near her chair could pull her straight into those pictures before she had time to think, and once the image started she would leave herself extra work, change seats, or keep moving so she would not have to sit with it.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
A smell, a tone of voice, or the simple discomfort of being too close to someone in a small room could pull her back into it. She would immediately look for the safest seat, sit with her back against a wall, or leave herself extra work to do so she would not have to stay with the image.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
When those cues hit, Marisol's mind did not stop at the memory itself; the old scene seemed to carry a verdict with it, and she would think, with a harsh certainty, that this was what it meant to be weak and trapped, that other people would have handled it better, and that she had somehow failed herself.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Even after she tried to push the memory away, the pictures seemed to sharpen and return, often in the very places where she had hoped to forget them.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
When one of those pictures came back during a staff meeting or while she was setting up folding chairs for a neighborhood event, she would answer messages, stack supplies, and keep her hands occupied, because the image felt less powerful when she was moving and more likely to swallow her whole if she stayed still.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
The more she pushed herself to keep moving, the less room there seemed to be for anything else, yet the memories still intruded.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Because she kept running from them in this way, every quiet pause at home or at her desk seemed to make the memory pop back up with greater force, and the bus stop, the conference table, and the narrow office hallway around the community center gradually became reminders in their own right.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
At work she would scan a meeting room before sitting, choosing the chair with the clearest view of the door or the seat that let her keep her back to a wall. On the bus home she found herself checking behind her at crosswalks and in shop windows, and at night she struggled to fall asleep because she needed to stay alert, as if lowering her guard might invite danger back in.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Living in that state of alertness made almost anything feel like a warning: a door left ajar at the center, a van parked too close to the curb, or a voice that rose suddenly in a tenant meeting could all make her feel that danger was near, and once she felt that way her mind went searching for the old scene again.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Over time, Marisol had come to believe that her reactions meant something bad about her. She told herself, with a flatness that sounded rehearsed, that she was weak, and that somebody else would have stopped the abuse from happening.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
That belief did not just shame her; it kept pulling the memory back into focus, as if she had to revisit the images to prove to herself where she had gone wrong, and the more she judged herself, the more vivid the room, the doorway, and the helplessness became.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
The problem was that this vigilance kept her close to the very sensations that set her off, and the more alert she became, the more the memory seemed to gather force. A sudden image would come to mind in the middle of a staff meeting, and with it came the thought that she was dead inside, cut off from feeling in a way that confirmed how damaged she believed herself to be.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
That same sense of danger also deepened the thought that something about her had been permanently altered; feeling this on edge all the time made her more certain that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe, and that conviction made the old pictures easier to summon whenever she tried to relax.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
As the months passed, the strategies she used to keep herself steady began to narrow her world. She stayed late at the community center to avoid taking the subway home with its unpredictable crowding.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Staying late at the center and taking the long way home gave her temporary relief, but each avoided route became its own reminder of what she could not bear; the emptying offices after hours, the train platform she no longer used, and the extra tasks she gave herself all kept the event arranged around her daily life, and that map of avoidance made the memory feel ever-present.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
She sat with her back to walls in restaurants, office trainings, and even family gatherings, and if she could not arrange that, she became restless and distracted. Yet these habits kept bringing the memories closer, not farther away.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
The more she organized her days around not being caught off guard, the more the ordinary places she entered seemed to carry the event with them, and each new detour or seat choice seemed to tell her again that the world was a place she had to survive rather than live in.
<<<END>>>
